question: What should you do if you receive a suspicious link from an unknown person?
explanation: Suspicious links can lead to fake websites or harmful software. Do not click them. Ignore and report them.

question: Which of these is the strongest password?
options: A long mix of words, numbers and symbols that only you know
explanation: Long passwords that mix words, numbers and symbols are hard to guess. Never use names, birthdays or simple numbers.

question: Someone calls and says they are from your bank and asks for the OTP sent to your phone. What should you do?
options: Give it so they can help you
Never share it and end the call
Share only half of the code
explanation: An OTP is private, like a key to your account. Real bank staff will never ask you for it.

question: Which is the safest way to use free public Wi-Fi?
options: Log in to your bank account quickly
Avoid banking and sensitive logins on public Wi-Fi
explanation: Other people on public Wi-Fi may be able to spy on your activity. Save banking and private logins for a trusted network.

question: What is a good privacy habit on social media?
options: Set your account to private and accept only people you know
Share your location live while you travel alone
explanation: Private accounts help you control who can see your photos and details. Strangers can misuse personal information.

question: Why should you install software updates on your phone?
options: They fix security problems and protect you
They make your phone slower on purpose
explanation: Updates close security gaps that criminals can use. Installing them keeps your phone and accounts safer.

question: What is two-factor authentication (2FA)?
options: An extra step, like a code, to prove it is really you
A way to share your account with a friend
A tool that deletes old messages
explanation: 2FA adds a second check. Even if someone learns your password, they still cannot get in without the extra code.

question: You get a message: “You won a prize! Pay a small fee to receive it.” What should you do?
options: Do not pay. Real prizes do not ask for money first
Forward it to everyone you know
explanation: Asking for a fee before giving a prize is a common scam. Do not pay and do not share your details.

question: Which of these should you NEVER share with anyone online?
explanation: PINs and passwords protect your money and accounts. Keep them to yourself, even from people you trust.

question: An email that looks like it is from your bank asks you to click a link and enter your details. It has spelling mistakes. What should you do?
options: Click the link and log in quickly
Do not click. Contact the bank using its official number or app
explanation: This is phishing. Fake messages copy real companies to steal your details. Always use the official app or number.

question: Why is using the same password on every account risky?
options: It is easy to remember, so it is always safe
If one site is hacked, criminals can open your other accounts
There is no risk at all
explanation: Criminals try stolen passwords on many websites. Use a different password for each important account.

question: A friend’s social media account suddenly asks you to send money urgently. What should you do?
options: Call your friend on a number you already know to check first
Give them your PIN so they can help
explanation: Hackers take over accounts and pretend to be friends. Confirm by calling the real person before sending anything.
